Brightwave discussed use of Redwood for behind-the-scenes audio automation, transcription, and episodic ad insertion. Problem: manual transcript/editing and ad insertion delays
Solution: Redwood inference for on-prem/private workflow and real-time drafts
Quantified impact: faster turnaround, lower cost per episode
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-07
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood), Jon (Redwood), Elliot (Redwood Producer), Lena (Brightwave), Marcus (Brightwave), Samir (Brightwave Eng), Priya (Brightwave Legal)

[00:00] Ava (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining — super excited, this is our customer story podcast recording with Brightwave. We might record live answers, but we also will use this for a short case study. can everyone say hi?
[00:18] Lena (Brightwave): hi, lena here, head of content at Brightwave, happy to be on — sorry about the slight echo, we're in a studio.
[00:25] Marcus (Brightwave): marcus here, producer, thanks for having us.
[00:31] Jon (Redwood): jon from redwood, i'll just kick off with a quick intro and then ava will lead the conversation.
[00:40] Ava: great — quick housekeeping: recording permission is on file, priya is here for legal if anything needs to be clarified. okay, lena, can you start by giving a short description of Brightwave and the podcast workflow you run?
[01:05] Lena: sure, so brightwave runs a network of six weekly shows, we have in-house editing and we do ad insertion, music beds, and transcripts for SEO — before redwood we were using a mix of manual transcription and a third-party cloud API, which introduced delays and some privacy concerns especially for paid ads and sponsor audio.
[01:40] Ava: interesting. can you quantify the bottleneck? like hours per episode?
[01:48] Lena: yeah, so editing workflow used to be about 10-14 hours per episode from raw audio to publish, a lot of that was waiting on transcripts and QA. sometimes we had to wait up to 24-36 hours because we were batching transcriptions.
[02:15] Marcus: and the ad insertion cycles would take an extra day because of manual QA on the segmented files.
[02:28] Ava: got it. jon, do you want to comment on how brightwave adopted redwood?
[02:35] Jon: sure. they started with a private deployment pilot — we set up a dedicated instance in their VPC so audio never left their cloud, used our streaming transcription + reranking to produce draft timestamps, and then used server-side inference to generate chapter markers and ad slots. the pilot let them cut the pipeline to about 3-4 hours per episode.
[03:05] Lena: yeah that's right, cutting down to 3 hours was massive; our producers could iterate multiple drafts in a single shift. we also liked the RBAC and audit logs — priya was very pleased.
[03:25] Priya (Brightwave Legal): yep just to note we reviewed the SOC2 docs and the audit trail, and the KMS integration met our policy for sponsor content.
[03:38] Ava: there was a part where we did a small cost/perf comparison — can you share the numbers you saw?
[03:45] Samir (Brightwave Eng): roughly we saw 40-55% cost reduction on processing per episode once we tuned batching and caching, that was mostly from the prefix caching and reduced token counts for generation tasks. throughput was stable on our GPU nodes.
[04:05] Elliot (Producer): i just want to flag, during the demo we played a sample of the chapter marker generation — there was a small transcription glitch at 1:42 where "ad slot" was transcribed as "add slot" but the semantic model corrected it in reranking; it's kind of typical, the human QA still catches small cases.
[04:32] Lena: yeah transcription is never perfect but the combined inference + human-in-the-loop worked well.
[04:40] Ava: nice. let's switch to a more conversational angle for the podcast — what's the story about how this changed your team's day-to-day?
[04:55] Lena: well, producers used to be reactive, waiting on overnight batches. now they proactively pull a draft right after recording, mark up the ad cues, and publish same-day for shorter shows. morale improved, too, because the team sees faster impact of edits.
[05:20] Marcus: and from a creative standpoint, being able to iterate quickly means we test more ad placements and measure listen-through, so sponsors are happier.
[05:37] Ava: any surprises during rollout?
[05:40] Samir: the main surprise was how much model quantization helped with cost on our on-prem GPUs — we weren't expecting such a neat drop without huge quality loss.
[05:52] Jon: quick plug, we recommended a mixed routing policy: dedicated for production spikes and hosted fallback for off-hours. that helped them avoid overprovisioning.
[06:10] Marcus: we did consider Descript for a while but we needed the custom inference for ad templates and private deployments; so redwood fit better.
[06:28] Ava: good callout. let's cover the technical integration at a high level for listeners who care about infra. samir, can you describe the pieces?
[06:36] Samir: sure — we ran redwood private in a small cluster in our VPC, we used the Redwood SDK to push audio chunks to the streaming endpoint, then used an internal queue to call chapter marker model and a separate reranker. KV cache was important for repeated prompts across episodes.
[07:05] Lena: and the team used the console for tracing when something failed which was helpful.
[07:12] Ava: listeners always like numbers — can you share concrete KPIs post-implementation?
[07:18] Lena: turnaround time down from 12-14h average to 3-4h; cost per episode processing down ~50%; sponsor conversion up 8% because we could experiment more.
[07:34] Marcus: publishers also like the audit trails — we can show sponsors when and where an ad was inserted which helped negotiations.
[07:46] Priya: also we enforced a retention policy in the private deployment which met our contracts.
[07:55] Ava: short aside — any vendor concerns during procurement?
[07:59] Lena: initially some leadership worried about vendor lock and reliance on a single runtime but the ability to pin model versions and export logs helped.
[08:12] Ava: nice. i want to include a micro-demo snippet — you ok with us playing the sample that jon mentioned earlier?
[08:19] Marcus: yes please.
[08:20] [08:20] Demo audio played (clip omitted from transcript)
[10:05] Elliot: after the clip, a couple production notes — small word swap in the transcript, but overall good.
[10:18] Lena: yeah, the clip shows the flow — we think it will make a good breakout on the podcast.
[10:25] Ava: moving towards audience questions i prepared: what advice would you give teams thinking about adopting redwood?
[10:34] Lena: start with a pilot on a non-customer-facing show, measure end-to-end time savings and iterate on prompts for your domain. don't expect perfect transcription at first, tune the reranker.
[10:46] Samir: also benchmark your sequence length distribution; if you have lots of long-form interviews, adjust kernel selection and batching.
[10:55] Jon: and set clear rollout policies — canary for a subset of episodes, fallback to hosted if on-prem is under pressure.
[11:05] Marcus: and involve legal early for music licensing.
[11:10] Ava: perfect. for the case study side, can you give a concise quote for the marketing blurb about impact?
[11:18] Lena: yeah, "Redwood helped Brightwave cut episode processing time by two-thirds, enabling same-day publishing and more sponsor experiments."
[11:30] Ava: excellent. i'll send a draft.
[11:34] [12:30] Conversation drifts into anecdotes about favorite podcast guests and sponsor stories; light laughter, filler.
[15:00] Marcus: quick timeline question — what does the onboarding timeline look like if we wanted to expand to full private infra for the whole studio?
[15:10] Jon: typical timeline is a 2-week pilot to validate workflows, then a 4-6 week roll to production depending on infra and compliance checks.
[15:25] Lena: who typically owns the infra work on redwood's side?
[15:30] Jon: our solutions engineers partner with your infra team; redwood provides a setup guide and we can do a remote pairing session.
[16:00] [20:00] Mid-call QA and clarifying questions about RBAC and SSO (SAML) integration; priya confirms SSO flows will meet Brightwave policy after some config.
[24:15] Ava: we also touched briefly on quantization profiles and how they trade off quality vs cost — samir, any more notes?
[24:30] Samir: we tested 4-bit and 8-bit profiles, found 4-bit with tuned kernels kept audio transcription quality acceptable for most parts, saved the most on cost.
[25:05] Lena: one hiccup was when a sponsor wanted the raw audio kept for two weeks only; we implemented a short retention window which the console enforced.
[25:25] Elliot: little production tip — keep a manual QA pass for the first two episodes after rolling out changes.
[30:00] Ava: ok nearing wrap-up — any final anecdotes or things you'd like in the episode?
[30:12] Lena: include a quick segment about our first sponsor success after the change — it was a short case where faster iteration allowed an A/B test that lifted listen-through.
[30:30] Marcus: and mention the audit trail feature because sponsors care.
[31:00] Ava: great. we're going to record a brief outro with lena and then stop the recording.
[31:12] [31:12] Short outro recorded
[32:00] Recording stopped, quick checks, thanks and confirm permissions.
[32:15] Ava: to recap next steps — we'll share the episode draft, one-pager, and permission form; you'll confirm music licensing and guest bios.
[32:30] Lena: sounds good.
[32:35] Marcus: we'll get bios and licensing by next week.
[32:40] Priya: i confirm legal is fine with this recording and will sign the permission.
[32:48] Ava: thanks everyone. end.
